nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How many environmental variables were utilized in predicting the potential distribution of Illicium griffithii?
nodes.answer: Fifteen environmental variables were utilized in the study.
nodes.paragraph: Predicting habitat suitability of Illicium griffithii under climate change scenarios using an ensemble modeling approach Anubhav Bhuyan1, Amal Bawri2, Bhrigu Prasad Saikia3, Shilpa Baidya1, Suhasini Hazarika1, Bijay Thakur1, Vivek Chetry4, Bidya Sagar Deka1, Pangkhi Bharali4, Amit Prakash1, Kuladip Sarma5 & Ashalata Devi1 Climate change is the most significant threat to global biodiversity , risking extinction for many species due to their limited adaptability to rapidly changing environmental conditions, such as temperature, precipitation, and other climate variables. Illicium griffithii , an endangered tree with ecological and medicinal value, remains understudied, particularly in Arunachal Pradesh. The aim of the study is to identify key environmental variables influencing the current distribution of I. griffithii and to predict the potential distribution under current and future climatic scenarios ( SSP245 and SSP585). We used an ensemble modeling approach that integrates five species distribution models ( SDMs). After multicollinearity test, we utilized fifteen environmental variables including bioclimatic variables, soil properties, topographical variables, and evapotranspiration to predict the potential distribution of I. griffithii . The study revealed that the current distribution is predominantly influenced by isothermality, nitrogen content at 0 5 cm depth, clay content at 0 5 cm depth, and seasonality of precipitation, with a total contribution rate of 42.6%.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life on land|Desertification mitigation|Indigenous plant species use_qna_002
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: How many species were identified in the comprehensive checklist of useful plants in Uganda?
nodes.answer: The checklist identified 1,37 species with known human uses.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract: Accelerating anthropogenic pressures threaten over two in five plant species globally with extinction, with an estimated 21% of threatened species on the IUCN Red List holding socio- economic value, imperiling species vital for global health. Important Plant Areas (IPAs) is an area- based conservation tool that recognizes the importance of useful species for human well-being and livelihoods. This study aims to identify hotspots of useful plants in Uganda using criterion B(iii) of the IPA framework. A comprehensive checklist of useful plants is presented, identifying 1,37 species with known human uses, equating to over one-fifth of vascular plant diversity in Uganda. A species richness analysis reveals a potential IPA network with 54 cells triggered using criterion B(iii). While Uganda S current protected area network contains a significant percentage (55%) of species on the useful plant checklist, the top 15 cells capture a higher number of species (59%) in a quarter of the total land area of the protected area network. Concerningly, 56% of Uganda S crop wild relatives are not recorded from the existing protected areas.

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What percentage of assessed threatened plant species has a known use according to the IUCN Red List?
nodes.answer: 21% of the assessed threatened plant species have a known use.
nodes.paragraph: Threatened and endemic species distribution correlates significantly with useful plant distribution, suggesting that countries with IPAs based upon threatened and endemic species could also capture useful plants. Keywords: Global Biodiversity Framework, Species richness, Useful plants, Conservation Introduction More than two in five plant species globally are threatened with extinction by accelerat- ing anthropogenic pressures (Bachman et al. 2024). Amongst these threatened species are many utilized by humans; the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species estimates that 21% of the assessed threatened plant species have a known use (IUCN 2023). Populations in developing nations often rely on wild-harvested plants used in traditional medicine as their primary healthcare (World Health Organization 2013), while socially, eco- nomically or culturally valuable plant species (henceforth useful plants for brevity) are also important in poverty reduction by enhancing Economic Botany, XX(X), 2025, pp. 1 20 2025, The Author(s)Received: 23 July 2024; accepted: 19 January 2025; published online Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https:// doi.

nodes.question: How many native vascular plants have been recorded in Uganda?
nodes.answer: At least 4816 native vascular plants have been recorded in Uganda.
nodes.paragraph: Such species can become displaced and threatened before their potential applications are recognized (Ulian et al. 2020). Uganda is one of the most biodiverse coun- tries in Africa (Plumptre et al. 2019). It is located at a meeting point of different major biogeographic elements of continental Africa, which is reflected in Uganda S diversity of vege - tation types and the presence of seven terrestrial ecoregions (Burgess et al. 2004; Fig. 1). This gives rise to a rich flora, with at least 4816 native vascular plants recorded (Kalema et al. 2016; Plumptre et al. 2019). Rural communities in Uganda depend heavily on plant diversity to fulfil a wide range of basic requirements, including, food, medicine, fuel and construction material (Barirega et al. 2012; Mollee et al. 2017 ; Tabuti et al. 2023 ). Land-use change for commercial agriculture, urbanization, industrialization and habitat degradation poses the greatest threats to plant diversity in Uganda. nodes.question: What dominant vegetation species were discovered in IREM according to the research?
nodes.answer: The dominant vegetation species in IREM are Dicranopteris pedata and Pinus massoniana.

The key to phytoremediation is selecting appropriate hyperaccumulators, and species that grow locally in IREM are generally the best choice. In comparison with traditional techniques, phytoremediation has some unique advantages such as cost-effectiveness, energy- efficiency, and environmental friendliness. Our previous field work discovered that the dominant vegetation species in IREM are Dicranopteris pedata (Houtt.) Nakaike and Pinus massoniana Lamb., the results confirm that Dicranopteris pedata can grow on acidic (pH 4 5), poor and dry soil due to its high nutrient- and water-use efficiency4,5. In fact, Dicranopteris pedata is a clonal plant which can asexually reproduce through underground stems. Subsequently, it demonstrates high survivability so that it can always form dominant communities at IREM in south China, and always form pure formations4.
